text_16ryz0h.value: What documents should a new homeowner keep?

text_992a54.value: Keep closing and insurance records in the appropriate secure place, plus appliance manuals, warranty documents, receipts, service history, contractor information, and equipment details you may need for repairs or claims.

text_63kvrv.value: What appliance information should I save after closing?

text_13xeciq.value: Record the brand, model number, serial number, approximate age or install date when known, warranty information, and a photo of the product label for major appliances and home systems.

text_1me70iz.value: Should I document smart-home devices left by the seller?

text_kmtr0p.value: Yes. Confirm ownership has been transferred or reset, then record the device name, location, model, and the household account responsible for it without storing passwords in plain text.

text_c8our2.value: Do I have to finish the whole checklist at once?

text_bih4fk.value: No. Start with HVAC, water heating, kitchen appliances, security, networking, and other expensive or frequently serviced equipment, then expand room by room.

text_uolcg2.value: Appliance labels are easy to ignore until a technician, parts site, warranty claim, or manual asks for the exact model. Use this guide to know where to look and what to save.

text_jpqy26.value: Why model and serial numbers matter

text_3st72r.value: The marketing name is often not specific enough. The model number identifies the exact product configuration a parts lookup or technician needs.

text_5dv550.value: Speed up warranty and service calls

text_1597myt.value: Support teams commonly ask for both model and serial number before confirming coverage, parts, recalls, or service options.

text_unq88l.value: The exact model is the fastest path to the right installation, care, troubleshooting, and owner documentation.

text_1u8frm7.value: Save the label once, use it for years

text_1h8vj68.value: Store model and serial numbers on the appliance record instead of relying on the label forever.

text_k658ke.value: Find the appliance record quickly when a technician or parts site asks for it.

text_1nlhtv6.value: Where to look on common appliances

text_1sd8cl7.value: Manufacturers vary, but rating plates and product labels tend to appear in predictable places. Check the label before moving or disconnecting an appliance.

text_2yddmk.value: Look inside the fresh-food compartment, along a side wall, near the crisper drawers, around the door frame, or behind the lower kick plate.

text_9fylrm.value: Open the door and inspect the inner door edge, frame, or side of the tub near the opening.

text_l7xkxm.value: Check the door or lid opening, rear panel, control-console area, or inside the door jamb.

text_1cmd5hf.value: Look around the oven door frame, storage drawer opening, rear panel, or underside of a removable cooktop area when the manufacturer directs it.

text_194l18v.value: The data plate is usually on the equipment cabinet or tank. Photograph it while access is clear and include install or service notes when known.

text_1mlgbbh.value: Appliance model and serial number FAQ

text_lavqjg.value: What to capture when you locate an appliance product label.

text_beucto.value: Is the model number the same as the serial number?

text_oik7ye.value: No. The model identifies the product type or configuration, while the serial number identifies the individual unit. Service and warranty teams may ask for both.

text_1na52f8.value: What should I do if the appliance label is faded?

text_1vtbjgt.value: Check purchase records, retailer order history, manufacturer apps, old service invoices, or documentation left with the home. Photograph any readable portion before it gets worse.

text_hkb915.value: Should I save a photo of the appliance label?

text_1y17t94.value: Yes. A clear label photo gives you the exact spelling and punctuation of the model and serial and can help when manually typed records contain an error.

text_1p29hgq.value: Why does the exact model number matter for manuals?

text_xwegzz.value: Appliance families often have several similar versions with different parts, controls, or installation requirements. The exact model helps you select the correct documentation.

text_zkbqve.value: Keep model and serial numbers in the broader household inventory.

text_1vetovi.value: Pair serials with coverage dates and proof of purchase.

text_7mytw6.value: Attach the correct paperwork to each appliance record.

text_z2eiq6.value: A home maintenance checklist you can actually keep up with.

text_g1s4h.value: Separate quick recurring checks from seasonal and annual work, record what was done, and follow the manufacturer instructions and professional guidance that apply to your home.

text_1naou5t.value: Build a maintenance rhythm instead of a giant to-do list

text_ua14ql.value: Check visible leaks or moisture, review the HVAC filter condition, test safety devices according to their instructions, and notice anything that changed.

text_1nabsi1.value: Review HVAC needs, exterior drainage, weather-sensitive equipment, outdoor devices, and other tasks that change with your climate and home.

text_2dcmyz.value: Revisit service history, manufacturer maintenance schedules, recurring professional inspections, warranties, and equipment nearing replacement age.

text_ymqu9p.value: Make maintenance part of the home record

text_1sklp9.value: Keep recurring home-care tasks visible instead of rebuilding a checklist each year.

text_1g1tml6.value: Record what was done, when it happened, and which device or home system it belongs to.

text_cvop5c.value: Keep filter sizes, model numbers, manuals, and warranty information next to the maintained equipment.

text_fa3351.value: Use this as a planning framework, not a substitute for the manual, local requirements, or a qualified professional. Your home may not contain every system listed.

text_16egvoy.value: Walk the home for visible leaks or moisture, inspect frequently used filters and vents, check drains, and test safety equipment on the schedule required by its manufacturer.

text_1yxycs2.value: Review cooling equipment, drainage, exterior water management, outdoor devices, screens, and weather-related wear before heavier warm-season use.

text_qqd737.value: Watch cooling performance, condensation and drainage, outdoor equipment, irrigation, and heat-sensitive electronics or networking gear.

text_9zgu2l.value: Prepare heating equipment, replace or inspect filters as needed, review exterior drainage, winterize appropriate outdoor systems, and document any service.

text_1i75ctx.value: Watch for moisture, freezing risk, heating issues, indoor air problems, and equipment that is working harder during cold weather.

text_funhzk.value: Review the service history for HVAC, water heating, appliances, alarms, electrical or plumbing concerns, and any manufacturer-specified maintenance you may have missed.

text_jxmxly.value: How to make a recurring home maintenance schedule manageable.

text_tccv62.value: What home maintenance should I do every month?

text_s3h79e.value: A short monthly inspection can include looking for leaks or moisture, checking filter condition, making sure drains and vents are functioning normally, and testing safety equipment according to the product instructions. Use your equipment manuals for exact service intervals.

text_op98lp.value: Should I replace my HVAC filter every month?

text_z007hy.value: Not automatically. Filter type, system use, pets, air quality, and manufacturer guidance affect replacement frequency. Inspect it regularly and follow the HVAC and filter manufacturer's recommendations.

text_cwcohv.value: How should I keep home maintenance records?

text_1wupftg.value: For each major system or appliance, keep the service date, what was done, provider or DIY notes, receipts when relevant, and the model or serial number tied to that work.

text_1lr2bpp.value: What is the easiest way to keep a maintenance checklist current?

text_32zrh7.value: Use recurring tasks and a service history tied to the actual equipment. That is easier to maintain than a static printable checklist that starts over every year.

text_yx59m3.value: Home Tech Vault started with a simple frustration: important information about a home was everywhere, except where you actually needed it.

text_11eksaa.value: Jason Eaton, founder of Home Tech Vault

text_fzwa64.value: I kept seeing the same problem: homeowners had the information, but no real place to keep it.

text_1nq3ejp.value: Manuals ended up in drawers. Receipts lived in email. Warranty information got lost. Service dates were written down somewhere — or not at all.

text_1s18gjt.value: The information existed, but it was scattered. And when something broke, when a warranty was needed, or when it was time to sell, finding the right detail became harder than it should have been.

text_hcwj4u.value: I started thinking about how much history a home quietly builds over time. Appliances get replaced. Systems get serviced. Rooms get updated. Documents get signed. Every year adds another layer.

text_t9uz5i.value: What if the home itself had one place to remember it all?

text_vdcex.value: HTV is meant to make homeownership feel a little easier.

text_1f2vkeq.value: Not by adding another complicated app to your life, but by giving your home a place for the details you'll eventually need.

text_1d80mth.value: The long-term idea is bigger than storing documents.

text_hsfa96.value: I want Home Tech Vault to become the living record of a home — something that becomes more useful the longer you own the property.

text_1ris7dv.value: When something breaks, you should know what it is. When something gets serviced, the history should be there. When you replace an appliance, that change should become part of the home's record.

text_f0c3k9.value: And when that home changes hands, the useful history should not have to disappear with the previous owner.

text_167f43x.value: Important information about your home should have one dependable place to live.

text_1vqbsat.value: When something breaks, expires, or needs service, the answer should be easy to find.

text_11kbi80.value: A home's useful history should stay with the home instead of disappearing over time.

text_1ml5384.value: “HTV is still growing, but the goal has stayed simple: make the information that comes with owning a home easier to keep, easier to find, and more useful over time.”

text_je53w4.value: One appliance, one receipt, one repair at a time.

text_kh0mxk.value: Appliances, fixtures, equipment and the details that came with them.

text_1lwu41q.value: Model numbers, purchase dates, manuals and receipts are useful right up until the moment you cannot find them. HTV keeps those details tied to the things they belong to.

text_u5ohvp.value: Repairs and service should not disappear after the technician leaves.

text_qvmyb1.value: A service visit becomes part of the history of the home. Keep track of what was done, when it happened and what might need attention next.

text_8o6usw.value: Receipts, warranties and invoices are only useful if you can find them.

text_1ujxpxp.value: Keep important proof together so you are not searching through old emails, drawers and filing cabinets when something goes wrong.

text_n33ye1.value: How to Organize Your Apple Devices

text_zqgm1m.value: A lived-in way to keep track of Apple devices across rooms and people — without another spreadsheet that dies in a week.

text_1bddqe8.value: Why Apple needs its own inventory lane

text_12ju8du.value: Mixed-brand lists are fine for a dashboard, but Apple support, warranties, and account recovery still ask brand-specific questions. Keeping a filtered view of Apple devices shortens those moments.

text_2xls14.value: Serial numbers live in Settings, About This Mac, or engraved on the device.

text_11bg4kk.value: Start with devices you can touch this week. Skip perfection. A partial Apple list that is accurate beats a complete fantasy spreadsheet.

text_p4nbna.value: What to capture on every device

text_y2ei9n.value: For Apple devices, prioritize fields that unlock support and claims:

text_c7xc3s.value:
• Apple ID email on the device
• model identifier (not just marketing name)
• serial number
• AppleCare status and end date
• Find My enrollment

text_1p6pupy.value: Add room, primary user, and purchase date when you know them. Leave blanks rather than guessing — wrong serials create worse support calls than missing ones.

text_1yih2ad.value: Map the Apple ID / iCloud footprint

text_1g55odk.value: Write down which household email owns which device in Apple ID / iCloud. Nobody remembers which Apple ID owns which iPad.

text_100mhor.value: If Family Sharing, Household, or shared-home features exist, note who is an owner versus a participant. That distinction matters when someone moves out or a phone is wiped.

text_qahrq6.value: Do not paste raw passwords into a shared inventory. Point to your password manager, and store non-secret context (account email, device nickname, recovery contact) beside the device record.

text_1gr1c5o.value: Assign each Apple device a room even if it travels. Traveling laptops can live under “Work bag” or a person’s name — consistency matters more than furniture accuracy.

text_1ttbo19.value: Trade-in and support chats stall without the serial.

text_11c5ywv.value: For shared living-room gear, pick one household owner for documentation purposes. That person is not the only user — they are the contact when warranties or replacements come up.

text_1dseoj2.value: Photograph serial labels, boxes if you still have them, and the device in its usual spot. Insurance and support both move faster with visuals.

text_1skrz5u.value: Attach receipts or order emails to the device record while they are still searchable. AppleCare+ dates matter more than the retail receipt once the first year ends.

text_1076yrm.value: If a device was a gift, note the giver and approximate date. Incomplete proof is still better than a blank history.

text_15wq9o2.value: Accessories that deserve a line item

text_umlrhh.value: Chargers, docks, remotes, and cases become orphaned fast. Add high-value or easy-to-confuse accessories as linked notes on the parent Apple device.

text_1kuh38c.value: When two family members own the same headphone model, label ownership in the inventory or you will solve the wrong warranty later.

text_14aumvo.value: Cables can stay generic unless they are proprietary and scarce — then a short note saves a reorder.

text_1gd47f6.value: Once Apple devices are listed, attach lightweight reminders: filter cleans, battery swaps, firmware check months, or AppleCare-style renewal windows.

text_6caj9l.value: HomeKit accessories vanish from memory when a hub changes.

text_naasbs.value: You do not need a corporate CMDB. You need dates and notes a tired human can follow on a Saturday morning.

text_1kuqm48.value: Make the list usable for someone else

text_1o32eio.value: Share a read-only view with a partner or house sitter for emergencies. They should be able to identify the living-room iPhone and find account ownership without hunting through texts.

text_1gwqvls.value: Review the Apple list after holidays and back-to-school — those are when devices arrive undocumented.

text_198wv4.value: Retire records when devices leave the house. A graveyard of sold phones creates false insurance totals.

text_1hsgrj5.value: Put it to work in Home Tech Vault

text_cmr4s6.value: Home Tech Vault is built for this exact household problem: devices, documents, and warranties in one place, with optional family sharing.

text_fbme9n.value: Create Apple device entries, attach receipts, and keep room/owner fields current. Related guides below cover warranties, serials, and smart-home specifics when those apply.

text_1xs5y55.value: Start with five devices today. Momentum beats a heroic weekend project.

text_157xalz.value: Do I need a separate list just for Apple?

text_9pd75k.value: Keep one household inventory, then filter by brand when you need it. Brand-specific guides help you capture the right Apple fields — they do not require a second system.

text_1te8zjq.value: What if I do not know the Apple ID / iCloud email?

text_1un9cho.value: Check the device settings or app that manages it, then write the email on the record. If you cannot sign in, note “unknown owner account” and fix it before the next OS update cycle.

text_1ueier3.value: Should passwords live in the inventory?

text_17pv8pp.value: No. Store passwords in a password manager. Keep inventory notes limited to account emails, device nicknames, and where the secret is stored.

text_8f998t.value: How detailed should Apple model names be?

text_1wd5h1w.value: Prefer the support model or identifier over the marketing nickname. model identifier (not just marketing name) is usually the field support asks for.

text_17pr13z.value: How often should we update the list?

text_9o38zi.value: Update when something arrives, leaves, or changes rooms. Do a 20-minute sweep each season to catch drift.

text_c8oqdm.value: Can kids help maintain the inventory?

text_1racpv0.value: Yes for non-sensitive fields like room and nickname. Keep warranty documents and account ownership with an adult.

text_etgr8v.value: When Home Tech Vault fits better

text_1l068uy.value: A Sortly Alternative Built for Home Inventory

text_1qn041r.value: Sortly is a flexible inventory platform. Home Tech Vault takes a more focused approach for homeowners — keeping devices, appliances, receipts, warranties, manuals, serial numbers, and purchase information together in one household vault.

text_1ohto35.value: Why homeowners look for a Sortly alternative

text_1vb29er.value: Sortly is built to handle broad inventory needs. That flexibility is valuable, but some homeowners do not need a full inventory-management platform to remember which television they bought, when the refrigerator warranty expires, or where the router receipt lives.

text_1wyd4lr.value: A household technology inventory has a narrower job: preserve the information that becomes important during repairs, warranty claims, support calls, replacements, moves, and insurance documentation.

text_1abo6k9.value: Home Tech Vault focuses its experience around that narrower problem. Instead of starting with generic inventory items, the system emphasizes devices, rooms, model numbers, serial numbers, warranties, receipts, manuals, maintenance, and household access.

text_1a328m1.value: General inventory vs home technology inventory

text_1xlsf38.value: Sortly can be used for home inventory, but its structure is broad enough to support everything from household belongings to professional equipment.

text_1cuc9ni.value: Home Tech Vault deliberately gives up some of that breadth in exchange for a more opinionated household technology workflow.

text_1fyc50t.value: If your inventory includes every possession, supply, tool, and box in storage, a broader inventory system may be appropriate. If your priority is appliances, electronics, smart-home devices, network equipment, warranties, receipts, and manuals, a specialized vault can reduce setup and maintenance.

text_1f4zc8l.value: Warranty tracking and proof of purchase

text_1x6p8ky.value: Knowing that you own an item is not enough when a warranty claim starts. You may also need the purchase date, model, serial number, receipt, warranty document, and other proof.

text_1sz9fb2.value: Home Tech Vault is structured around keeping those records close to the device they belong to rather than treating them as unrelated files.

text_cezl8p.value: That difference matters most when something fails unexpectedly. The goal is to open one record and find the information needed for support instead of searching email, cloud drives, drawers, and old boxes.

text_1vl6hwt.value: Receipts and manuals are easy to save and surprisingly hard to find months or years later.

text_15wdp6p.value: A household-focused inventory works best when documents remain attached to the device context: which refrigerator the receipt belongs to, which television the warranty covers, and which router a manual describes.

text_wsj8ry.value: Home Tech Vault emphasizes that relationship so the inventory acts as more than a list of things you own.

text_ou1h4p.value: Built around a household instead of an asset database

text_kugqef.value: Many inventory platforms are designed with businesses, warehouses, equipment, or professional asset tracking in mind.

text_1f77sin.value: Home Tech Vault uses a household mental model instead: devices live in rooms, family members may need access, warranties have expiration dates, and documents exist because someone may need them during a real-world problem.

text_gjk39u.value: That narrower experience can be easier for families that want organization without turning home inventory into another system they need to administer.

text_1gi0n14.value: Which is better: Sortly or Home Tech Vault?

text_uc001d.value: Choose Sortly when flexibility and broad inventory management are the priority.

text_16tlxrb.value: Choose Home Tech Vault when the inventory is primarily about household technology, appliances, warranties, receipts, manuals, serial numbers, and related records.

text_6c30ft.value: The deciding question is not which product has more inventory features. It is whether you need a general inventory platform or a purpose-built home technology vault.

text_1tv6a8k.value: Sortly is a strong fit for users who need broad inventory management across many kinds of assets.

text_1gfe2vg.value: Home Tech Vault is designed for a narrower customer: homeowners who want important technology information organized before something breaks.

text_1me3fi1.value: If your main frustration is finding receipts, warranty information, manuals, serial numbers, and device details, the specialized workflow may be more useful than a general-purpose inventory system.

text_19dhemz.value: What Home Technology Information Should You Keep? A Homeowner's Checklist

text_1hi6uzz.value: Learn what technology information every homeowner should save, including device serial numbers, receipts, warranties, manuals, Wi-Fi information, and maintenance records.

text_e5boc0.value: A practical homeowner checklist for keeping the technology information you will actually need later.

text_y2jv40.value: Record the model number for major electronics, appliances, networking equipment, and smart-home devices. The model number identifies the exact version of the product you own and is often the fastest way to find correct support information.

text_xsf7dg.value: Model numbers are useful when searching for manuals, replacement parts, firmware instructions, accessories, compatibility information, and manufacturer support. Two products that look almost identical may use completely different parts or documentation.

text_qfwbhu.value: For equipment that will eventually be mounted, installed, or difficult to reach, capture the model number before installation.

text_12i0os7.value: Serial numbers are unique to individual devices and are frequently required for warranty claims, manufacturer support, repairs, insurance documentation, product registration, and some recall programs.

text_qk61qf.value: Take a clear photograph of the serial-number label when you install or purchase an important device. This is especially helpful for televisions mounted to walls, appliances pushed into cabinets, networking equipment stored in closets, and other products whose labels may become difficult to reach.

text_1q9hsz6.value: Do not wait until a device fails to discover that its serial number is printed somewhere inaccessible.

text_s55cja.value: Keep the purchase date for important devices whenever possible. Even an approximate date is better than no record, but an exact purchase date makes warranty and replacement decisions much easier.

text_1q8sqdk.value: Purchase dates can help you determine warranty eligibility, expected device age, replacement timing, maintenance history, and whether a product has lasted as long as expected.

text_bx98nk.value: When you buy something new, adding the purchase date while the receipt is still in front of you takes seconds.

text_ansqug.value: Receipts are one of the easiest records to lose and one of the most frustrating records to need later. Many warranty claims require proof that you purchased the product and when the purchase occurred.

text_xjo4mu.value: Save digital receipts directly. For paper receipts, photograph or scan them before the print fades. Keep the receipt connected to the device record rather than buried in a general folder where you will have to search for it later.

text_zhfj1s.value: Proof of purchase can also be useful for returns, insurance documentation, resale, and tracking what you originally paid.

text_52oc7a.value: Knowing that something probably has a warranty is not enough. Record who provides the coverage, when coverage began, when it expires, and whether an extended protection plan exists.

text_ei47pb.value: Useful warranty details include the manufacturer, retailer or protection-plan provider, coverage period, expiration date, claim instructions, and any documents required to make a claim.

text_1bh9ae.value: A warranty is most valuable when you can identify it before paying for a repair or replacement.

text_n04cns.value: You do not need a drawer filled with paper manuals. For most devices, a digital copy or reliable link to the correct official manual is easier to keep and easier to search.

text_1x24m0i.value: Manuals become useful when you need troubleshooting steps, maintenance recommendations, reset instructions, specifications, error-code explanations, replacement-part information, or setup guidance.

text_rpc7nl.value: The important part is associating the correct manual with the exact device model you own.

text_126hb9h.value: Your home network has become basic household infrastructure. If the internet stops working, having a simple record of how the network is structured can save a surprising amount of troubleshooting time.

text_atpyhc.value: Useful network documentation can include your internet provider, modem model, router model, mesh equipment, access-point locations, equipment ownership, installation notes, and important configuration details.

text_5xn6b3.value: Avoid turning a general home record into an unsecured plain-text password list. Sensitive credentials should remain protected appropriately. The goal here is to document how the network works and what equipment belongs to it.

text_1yexwdg.value: If a professional installed or serviced something in your home, record who did the work and when. This is particularly useful for security equipment, networking, cameras, thermostats, smart-home systems, HVAC-connected technology, and specialty installations.

text_171h8zb.value: Keep the company name, service date, contact information, work performed, and any useful notes. If a problem returns later, you will know who worked on it and what was changed.

text_1i82j32.value: Service history also helps another homeowner, family member, or technician understand what happened previously.

text_19i3evk.value: Some technology requires periodic care even when nothing appears wrong. Batteries need replacing, firmware needs updating, filters need changing, electronics need cleaning, and occasionally equipment needs professional service.

text_grvycq.value: A simple maintenance history can include firmware updates, battery changes, filter replacements, cleaning, repairs, service visits, and major configuration changes.

text_mvyu7k.value: You do not need to record every tiny action. Focus on anything you might reasonably ask yourself later: When did I last do this?

text_18llc16.value: Home technology increasingly comes with recurring services. Security monitoring, cloud camera storage, internet service, software, extended protection, and other subscriptions can become part of the cost of owning a device.

text_1mwebtp.value: Keep a record of the service name, the device or household function it supports, renewal timing, and where the subscription is managed.

text_1g48v2k.value: This makes it easier to understand recurring household technology expenses and prevents subscriptions from continuing long after the related device has disappeared.

text_cy0qn1.value: How should you organize all of this?

text_nw1lbe.value: The best system is the one your household will actually maintain. A spreadsheet, cloud folder, notes app, traditional home binder, or dedicated home technology organizer can all work.

text_6o37hk.value: Whatever system you choose, avoid scattering different parts of the same device across multiple places. A useful device record should make it easy to move from the product itself to its receipt, warranty, manual, service history, and other supporting information.

text_1pf78id.value: Start with the expensive or important technology in your home rather than attempting to document everything in one weekend. Your router, major appliances, televisions, computers, security equipment, and smart-home hubs are good places to begin.

text_fywzh0.value: Create a digital memory for your home

text_1v8cad4.value: Home Tech Vault was built around this exact problem: important home technology information usually exists, but it lives in too many different places.

text_1rdt82f.value: Home Tech Vault gives homeowners one place to organize devices, documents, receipts, warranties, manuals, Home Wi-Fi information, subscriptions, and maintenance history so the information is available when it is actually needed.

text_t2fvci.value: You do not need a perfect inventory on day one. Start with a few important devices, capture the records that would be difficult to recreate, and build the household record over time.

text_lx2on9.value: If you are not sure where your home technology documentation currently stands, the free Home Tech Health Check can help identify the biggest gaps first.

text_fmm0xf.value: What technology information should every homeowner keep?

text_13rz9jc.value: At minimum, keep model numbers, serial numbers, purchase dates, receipts, warranty details, manuals, important network equipment information, and meaningful maintenance or service history for your most important devices.

text_10jtxk8.value: Should I keep paper manuals for every device?

text_fozjjr.value: Usually not. A digital copy or reliable link to the official manual is often easier to organize and search. Keep paper copies only when they provide something you cannot easily reproduce digitally.

text_1lhuzc1.value: Is it safe to keep Wi-Fi information with home records?

text_1q2boae.value: Documenting your network equipment, provider, locations, and configuration context is useful. Avoid storing sensitive passwords in unsecured plain-text documents.

text_18hj7o7.value: Which devices should I document first?

text_195n5wb.value: Start with expensive, important, difficult-to-access, or infrastructure-related devices such as major appliances, televisions, computers, routers, security equipment, thermostats, cameras, and smart-home hubs.

text_19km16.value: How often should home technology records be updated?

text_1iwak2.value: Update records when you buy, replace, sell, repair, or substantially reconfigure a device. A quick household review once or twice a year can catch anything you missed.
